Bob Lewis Photo
Co-promoters John Kaishian (left) and Tom Marchese guide the huge Wisconsin Auto
Racing operation so all runs smoothly and the fans can have an enjoyable afternoon
of the finest in professional auto racing.
Milwaukee is one of the auto racing capitals of the world. Proof of it is today's United States Auto
Club national championship late model stock car race. It is one of the few major racing events held
on a non-holiday weekday afternoon.
We thank you for spending the day with us. Many of you took off work or decided to spend an
afternoon of your vacation at the Wisconsin State Fair Speedway. We know you will not be disap-
pointed, as the races on the famed Milwaukee mile always provide plenty of action and good, hard racing.
Today's race is the second of three held during the Wisconsin State Fair. The first was the 150-mile
stock car event scheduled for last Sunday. On this Sunday, Aug. 23, the 200 mile, 10th annual Tony
Bettenhausen Classic for championship (Indy) cars,will end the fair. The next stock car race, a 250-mile
event, is scheduled for Sunday, Sept. 13. We hope to see you at both.
Should you have any comments on today's race, please feel free to contact us.
Sincerely,
John Kaishian, Tom Marchese

BAY
One of the most
consistent drivers
on the USAC stock
car circuit has to be
Wilbur "Bay" Dar-
nell of Deerfield,
Ill., who is now in
his ninth year of
competition in the
stocks.
Russ Lake Photo
A veteran of short track racing in northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin, Darnell was a frequent competitor
on the old quarter-mile Fair Park dirt oval, having credit for one modified feature win on that track.
In 1962 he drove his first USAC stock car race in a 1961 Ford. He gained little more than experience that
first year, finishing 21st in the point standings. He displayed steady improvement, however, and by 1966, he fin-
ished sixth in the standings with an equally high showing in 1967.
Darnell drove his first USAC Championship car event in 1965, placing ninth at DuQuoin, Ill. He continued
driving the smaller cars until early in the 1968 season when he was badly burned in an accident at Milwaukee in
June which took the life of Ronnie Duman.
Though it took a while for him to regain his old form, he was back in action by the end of 1968.
He ranks 13th in the all-time USAC stock car point standings and, although he has often been a front-runner, he
is still looking for his first USAC late model victory.
